Q1400866.summary: This photograph shows the front of the little Anglo-Saxon casket, framed by runic inscriptions: at the left the pagan legend of Weland the Smith, at the right the Magi approaching the enthroned Virgin with the Christ Child on her lap, led by a large star. Set side by side, the grim tale and the Nativity offering suggest the passage from the old heroic world to the new light of Christ. It is one of the earliest English images of the infant Christ.
facts: The Magi are identified by a runic label reading 'magi'; the Adoration is the only Christian scene on the casket, which also shows Romulus and Remus and Titus's capture of Jerusalem.
The runic inscription around the front panel is a riddle about the casket's own material, the bone of a stranded whale.

Augustus Wollaston Franks gave the panels to the British Museum in 1867; the missing right end panel turned up in Auzon, France, was sold to the Bargello in Florence and was recognised as part of the casket in 1890.
Q1400866.notes: Christ appears only as a small figure in the Adoration scene at the right of the front panel. 'Whalebone' here means whale bone, not baleen.

cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: On a dark hillside, the haloed Christ stands with both hands raised while a crowned ruler and soldiers, one swinging a sword, press toward him from the left. The miniature closes Psalm 4 just before the opening of Psalm 5.
facts: Its pictures interpret the psalms literally, historically or — very often — Christologically, as prophecies of the life of Christ.
The manuscript came to Württemberg under Duke Charles Eugene (its sale is first mentioned in 1787) and has been in the library at Stuttgart since at least 1818.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature. The precise verse illustrated is not certain; the scene shows Christ confronted by his enemies.

cur:monumental-castelseprio-adoration-ma.summary: The Magi, in Phrygian caps and swirling cloaks, press forward from the left to offer their gifts to the Christ Child, who sits on the Virgin's lap at the right; an angel and the star appear above. The scene is partly damaged, but its movement and colour remain vivid.
facts: The frescoes of Santa Maria foris portas were rediscovered under later plaster only in 1944; their date and the origin of their painter remain controversial, though the first half of the 9th century is increasingly favoured.
They show strong Byzantine influence combined with a freedom of handling recalling late antique painting, and are often described as the finest early medieval pictorial cycle in Italy.

Q116272738.summary: Christ sits frontally on a cushioned throne set between columns, blessing with his raised right hand and resting his left on a closed book on his knee, his head framed by a large cross-nimbus. Above, two apostles lean out over the canopy, as if from balconies, to look on. The calm, classical figure, framed by a border of acanthus, reflects the Carolingian desire to recover the dignity of early Christian art.
facts: The Met dates the plaque to 850–875 and attributes it to northern France (accession 17.190.41, gift of J. Pierpont Morgan, 1917).
It is the same size (14.5 × 8.8 cm) and shares the same framing and throne design as The Met's plaque with the enthroned Virgin and Child (17.190.39), with angels in place of apostles above.
Q116272738.notes: Whether the two Met plaques originally belonged to the same object (e.g., a book cover) was not verified.

wga:zearly/2/2paintin/0rome1.summary: Christ hangs alive on a broad cross, eyes open and arms outstretched, dressed in a long dark purple colobium edged with gold, beneath a titulus in Greek letters and a crescent moon in the night sky. The Virgin and Saint John, labelled in Latin, stand to either side; between them the soldier Longinus, named in the inscription, points his lance and Stephaton raises the sponge beside a small bucket. Painted for the chapel of Theodotus in Santa Maria Antiqua, it is one of the most important images of the Crucifixion to survive from 8th-century Rome.
facts: The fresco is the centrepiece of the chapel of Saints Quiricus and Julitta, decorated at the expense of Theodotus, an official of the church, during the pontificate of Pope Zacharias (741–752).
Christ's sleeveless colobium is an eastern element, which the Web Gallery of Art notes is otherwise known mainly from Syrian manuscripts.
Santa Maria Antiqua was buried by an earthquake in 847, which helped preserve its paintings; it was uncovered after the church above it was demolished in 1900.
wga:zearly/2/2paintin/0rome1.notes: The WGA classes the painter as 'Pre-Romanesque Painter (Italian)'; the style is strongly Byzantine. The same image appears as commons:18265619 (marked as duplicate).
